newsitem.title: USA: Powder hounds consult net before heading to slopes.
newsitem.headline: Powder hounds consult net before heading to slopes.

text.p: Your skis are waxed and strapped to the car, your other gear is stowed in the trunk. You've grabbed breakfast and enough cash for a lift ticket and lunch. Only one thing to do before heading for a glorious day on the slopes -- get online to double check the snow report.
Snow reports are just the beginning. For skiers and snowboarders, the Internet and online services offer resources as deep -- and fun -- as a slicing through fresh powder.
The 1996-97 ski season has witnessed a proliferation of Web sites and e-mail services devoted to skiing, snowboarding and other cold-weather outdoor activities.

Sites that have been around for a season or more are adding features such as online stores and reservations services. One start-up Web business even helps people design their own high-performance skis.
Some skiers have made the Internet a key part of pre-ski rituals.
"I haven't used the Internet much, but I do use it for ski info .... mainly to check ski conditions or wherever I am planning a trip," said Julie Gauntt, of Washington state.

Greg Lister, 19, a college freshman in Ottawa, Canada, and long-time skier, hangs out in places like AMI News' On The Go Ski+Snowboard Report (http://www.aminews.com/ski/) to quiz other skiers about snow conditions and nightlife at resorts he wants to visit.
"I tend to value their reports more than the facts on the resorts' home pages," Lister said.

AMI is an Internet old-timer, in the middle of its third ski season on the Web. The Orinda, Calif., company's Internet service is an outgrowth of its mainstay business producing daily ski reports on 250 North American resorts for 1,500 radio stations and newspapers around the country.

Online, AMI supplies similar reports to 15 Web sites including Yahoo Ski Report (http://la.yahoo.com/external/ami), Ski Travel Online (http://www.skito.com/) and SkiNet (http://www.skinet.com/), from the publisher of Ski and Skiing magazines.
AMI's own page mixes ski reports with snappy columns on destinations, gear, the pro racing circuit, snowboarding and other topics, plus a public message forum.
Traffic at the site has grown 50 percent since last year, to more than 125,000 visitors a month, said Chad Dyer, AMI's Internet services director.
"The demographics of the Internet are a perfect fit with the demographics of skiing," both attracting well-educated, well-paid men and women ages 18 to 40, Dyer said.

InterZine's two sites, iSki (http://www.iski.com/) and Snowboarding Online, or SOL (http://www.solsnowboarding.com/) -- both of which are duplicated on America Online -- are two other major contenders.

iSki features news, forums, snow reports, online shopping, and an online travel desk. SOL targets Gen-X shredders with chats, event and racing news, columns and periodic "Cyber SOL" tours of favourite snowboard resorts.

A newcomer going ski to ski with AMI and iSki is SnowBytes, a free service that delivers snow conditions to a subscriber's e-mailbox. Mercury Mail, the Denver e-mail news company, rolled out SnowBytes in mid-December and already has close to 20,000 subscribers.

Skiers fill out a personal profile that outlines the resorts they want to track and how often they want reports. Subscribers can also sign up for reports on World Cup racing and ski tips, and "First Tracks," an early morning alert when four or more inches of snow has dumped on their favourite ski hill.

Nearly all the major ski resorts in the United States have Web sites loaded with everything from ski conditions to lodging reservations to hours at the on-site day-care centre. Some display pictures of popular runs taken by "ski cams," outdoors-mounted video cameras.

My Ski's (http://www.myski.com/) build-your-own-ski service is a joint venture between Customised Internet Technologies in Los Altos, Calif., and high-performance ski maker Evolution in Salt Lake City. Visitors to the site input their ability level and receive recommendations for Evolution skis that match. A special "dashboard" allows them to select the colour, graphics and lettering they want on the skis, which run more than $600.
Other ski sites of interest:
-- Alpine World Club 1997 (http://www.alpcom.it/ski/) -- Mens and womens schedules and standings, points lists, earnings and a photo archive.
-- Outside Online's Ski Reports (http://outside.starwave.com/places/skiarea/skiindex.html) -- Snow reports, chat rooms race results and news.
-- Ski Travel Online (http://www.skito.com/) -- Snow reports, destinations, package deals and a mystery contest, "Murder on the Mountain."
-- Alberto Tomba (http://www.alberto.tomba.it/) -- A self-built monument to the Italian ski sex symbol written in Italian and English, with audio and video highlights of Tomba La Bomba's best races.
-- Usenet newsgroups devoted to skiing include rec.skiing, rec.skiing.alpine, and rec.skiing.nordic.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
